chat.author: Mike Bishop
chat.text: Agreed, there are a number of cases where you really want to make sure e.g. the unidirectional stream header is received and processed. Consider everyone's beloved Server Push, if you don't read the push stream header far enough to associate it with an existing PUSH_PROMISE, there are state tracking problems.

chat.author: Kazuho Oku
chat.text:
As to if this fits into HTTP semantics, at the moment, when facing a short response, proxies in production needs to choose between: a) send RESET to downstream (loses bytes!) , b) forward the bytes being received and send FIN (hiding the error).
Users complain for _b_ (but not _a_), so without RESET_STREAM_AT, we _are_ hiding errors.

chat.author: Alan Frindell
chat.text: Kazuho: But FIN for an HTTP response has a semantic which is -- you received the complete response.  If you convert a RST to a FIN, you might be poisoning a downstream cache

chat.author: Dennis Jackson
chat.text: Unlinkable 0-RTT for TLS: Stick a HPKE key in DNS. The client uses that HPKE to mint its own 0-RTT PSK. The handshake proceeds as normal (with cert and its own key exchange and the psk mixed in).

chat.author: Dennis Jackson
chat.text: Normally in TLS PSKs, the server wraps the PSK symmetrically. In this unlinkable 0-RTT variiant, the client wraps it asymetrically. Unlinkability ought to hold up to the consistency of the HPKE key (like in OHTTP)

chat.author: Dennis Jackson
chat.text: Design sketch provided without warranty, implication of suitability, security or deployability etc etc etc

chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: (And stick a signature on the HPKE key in DNS)

chat.author: Ted Hardie

chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: @Ted You can stick a WebPKI signature on the HPKE public key before putting it in DNS

chat.author: Dennis Jackson
chat.text: In both OHTTP and this variant of 0-RTT TLS, you need to authenticate the HPKE key. OHTTP doesn't give you this out of the box either.

chat.author: Martin Thomson
chat.text: This can be delivered over HTTPS instead.  Avoiding DNS for this seems sensible.

chat.author: Martin Thomson

chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: Regarding the comparison with TLS 0-RTT: Use of 0-RTT is strongly opt-in at the layer above TLS.  In Chunked OHTTP, we're in the opposite situation, where the 0-RTT flight is already in use carrying application data.  Changing the Chunked OHTTP "abstract interface" to make 0-RTT opt-in would help a lot.

chat.author: Christopher Wood
chat.text: Sure: the solution here is so trivial: send ephemeral public key use it for PFS. Couple that with frequent config rotation, you have a reasonable story for PFS altogether. For TLS, we don't have a way to advertise or distribute a public key for unlinkable 0-RTT. We'd need to build that, either in band or out of band, and tackle the same problems that OHTTP deployments have already solved for distributing and authenticating this public key. PFS for the request is a key management problem that TLS has not solved but OHTTP has, whereas PFS for the response is a native TLS feature that we can solve with OHTTP, and the relative cost of making this OHTTP change is less than the cost of making the TLS change
